description: A multidisciplinary team of engineers, designers, and space enthusiasts at NASA Space Apps 2026. Combining full-stack development with NASA open data, we build smart navigation and survival systems to guide future astronauts safely across the extreme Martian terrain
summary:
Marswalk Explorer is an interactive tactical planetary mapping and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) navigation web application developed for the first human explorers on Mars. While NASA’s robotic planetary archives are vast, current tools operate predominantly at regional or global scales without real-time astronaut mobility constraints.

Marswalk Explorer addresses this challenge by integrating multi-mission NASA datasets including MGS MOLA topography, MRO CTX high-resolution imagery, and Viking color mosaics rendered under the official Mars Coordinate Reference System (IAU_2015:49900). The platform enables astronauts and mission controllers to plot terrain-aware routes across Jezero Crater, evaluate cross-sectional elevation profiles, calculate 24-hour solar incidence angles, and monitor surface environmental telemetry.

This system is vital because spacesuit mobility is severely constrained. By actively mitigating steep slope hazards (>15°) and hazardous dust traps while optimizing astrobiological sampling routes, Marswalk Explorer ensures safer, scientifically optimized human exploration on the Red Planet.
details:
1. What does it do & How does it work?

Marswalk Explorer is an aerospace-grade tactical planetary mapping and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) navigation platform developed for astronauts exploring Jezero Crater (18.44° N, 77.45° E), Mars.

How it works:

  • Planetary Projection Engine (IAU_2015:49900): Eliminates Earth-based WGS-84 distortions by projecting spatial layers directly onto the true Martian sphere radius (R=3,396,190 mR = 3,396,190\text{ m}R=3,396,190 m) using OpenLayers and proj4js with Mars Equirectangular 2×12 \times 12×1 tiling (EPSG:104905).
  • Multi-Mission Layer Compositing: Streams and blends verified WMTS tile services from NASA Mars Trek combining MGS MOLA elevation shaded relief, MRO CTX high-resolution (5 m/px) context mosaics, and Viking MDIM 2.1 natural color imagery.
  • Terrain & Slope-Aware Pathfinding: Evaluates sub-kilometer DEM raster elevation grids in real time. As waypoints are plotted, the engine calculates cumulative distance, ascent/descent, and local slope angles.
  • JPL Solar Ephemeris & Telemetry Modeling: Simulates 24-hour diurnal solar azimuth and elevation angles via NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data, while pulling surface weather parameters (sol clock, ground temperature, atmospheric pressure) based on MSL REMS and Perseverance MEDA archives.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Crew Safety First: Spacesuits severely constrain mobility. The platform actively flags impassable slope hazards (>15∘–20∘>15^\circ\text{–}20^\circ>15∘–20∘) and hazardous dust traps (e.g., Séítah dunes), preventing falls or rover immobilization.
  • Offline Field Autonomy: Functions client-side, enabling astronauts to make real-time routing decisions despite the 4-to-24-minute Earth-Mars communication latency.
  • Maximized Science Return: Overlays astrobiological targets (hydrated clays, delta scarps, carbonates) directly on traversal paths, allowing crews to maximize sample value within strict oxygen and power budgets.
  • Standardized Mission Export: Exports complete flight plans with waypoints, coordinates, elevation, slope, and life support estimates into standard .csv files ready for GIS tools (QGIS, ArcGIS) and mission spreadsheets.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Marswalk Explorer establishes an open-source, reproducible standard for planetary surface navigation interfaces. Its intended impact is to transition from passive orbital observation to active, astronaut-centric field navigation—serving as a foundational framework adaptable for future NASA crewed missions, astronaut Augmented Reality (AR) helmet visors, and autonomous pressurized rover guidance.

4. How is your project creative?

  • Dual Synchronized Profiler: Simultaneously visualizes cross-sectional terrain elevation alongside 24-hour solar incidence curves, helping crews anticipate sunlit working windows and shadowed cold traps.
  • Tactical Mission Control HUD: Designed specifically with high-contrast, low-fatigue aerospace UI tokens optimized for high-glare environments inside Martian pressurized suits or habitat modules.
  • Hybrid Modular Architecture: Pairs an ultra-fast Next.js frontend with an independent Python FastAPI geospatial backend that can run offline or on local rover compute nodes.

5. What factors did your team consider?

  • Martian Geodesy vs. Earth GIS: Standard GIS tools default to Earth's WGS-84 datum. We strictly enforced Mars IAU Sphere specifications to ensure metric distances and slope calculations are physically accurate.
  • Astronaut Physiological Constraints: Incorporated oxygen consumption rate modeling and terrain-adjusted walking speeds (~1.2 to 3.8 km/h dependent on slope incline).
  • Communication Latency: Ground control at Houston cannot guide real-time walking steps; every telemetry calculation and routing mechanism was designed for standalone local execution.

6. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software

  • Frontend Framework: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16 (Turbopack), Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend & GIS Engine: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, NetworkX, Uvicorn.
  • Mapping & Geodesy: OpenLayers 10, Proj4js (IAU_2015:49900).
  • NASA Data Protocols & APIs: NASA Mars Trek WMTS, JPL Horizons Ephemeris API, USGS Astrogeology, NASA PDS Atmospheres.
